I have worked for the same company for 12 years, starting off as a parts driver and climbing the ladder to my current position as estimator. I have installed exhibits from Wyoming to NYC to Washington DC(and a bit beyond).
[IAMA] I make museum exhibits for a living AMA

What kind of museum? History, art, etc?

What exhibit did you enjoy making the most?

All kinds, I have worked on galleries for paintings, memorials, history museum, nature centers, zoos, visitor centers, and children learning centers.

My favorite to work on was for the Bethel Woods Performing Arts Center, which is where the original Woodstock concert was held and was the main focus of the exhibit. We had to psychedelic paint jobs done for that, one on an old school bus that we had converted to a theater and the other was a VW beetle.

What is the most disastrous looking piece you have had to install?
What was the coolest?

Bonus points for pics. We would like to see your work.

The coolest i have mentioned before was the Bethel Woods Woodstock Museum there is a video that shows some of the exhibit on this page http://www.bethelwoodscenter.org/the-museum

The most disastrous looking would be the 9-11 Memorial Museum at Ground Zero, it is beautiful but has the most disastrous images. As far as bad exhibits, those are usually because the client wants to save money and have us do the basic work. For example a childrens learning center didn't have a big budget but wanted an interactive about core sample that was a wall with pockets for cylinders that would represent the core samples. To save some money they wanted to paint it themselves, which did look disastrous.
The woodstock museum reminds me of one of the Colonial Williamsburg museums, except with more hippies. That was a well put together environment.
It was an amazing design that I wish we could take credit for. The intro timeline and radio exhibits were pretty cool in my opinion.
What tools and skills have been the most helpful for your career?

Well doing what I was asked every time, as a parts driver I was willing to make long hauls by myself when ever they were needed. I was willing to sleep in the truck(these are not semis with sleeper cabins but box trucks) to save time and money. When working in the warehouse I was there whenever asked for over time and when I was offered to work in the shop helping the manager I jumped at it. In most of the area's I worked in I had little to no experience but put in the effort to learn it quickly which is what has helped push me along, managment here prefers to promote from within whenever possible.
What do you always carry with you for work, specifically what tools do you always rely on (e.g. laptop vs tape measure)

I carry my phone these days, it can take pictures for questions which is really helpful. It's also a calculator, can search the web and play podcasts. A tape measure is useful which is why I have one in my office, but as an estimator I work more off of drawings then any actual items to be measured.

no, just pulled away to deal with something. Ill get back to the questions in a about 20 minutes.

Sounds like the business is pretty steady. How is this work contracted out? Do you have contracts with specific museums or do they ask for quotes based on what they need? Also, do you normally have to do the installations at night when the museum is closed?

It is not steady, the recession a few years back almost destroyed us and we are still feeling it. Most museums with the exception of the Smithsonian Institute museums are usually through donors or some kind of funds. Many of which were tied to real estate which when that bubble popped dried up a lot of funding. Contracting for museums happen a few ways, there are times when we are contracted to design and build a museum but those are much less common and normally only happens after a museum has worked with you and enjoyed the results. The most common is a museum will hire a design firm to create a design for their space and then send that out to bid to a number of companies like mine that will estimate the cost to buy materials, construct, paint, deliver and install. Night time installations do happen but are less frequent because of the up charge to labor rates for working over night, most often the museum will close off a wing and have a specific time for bringing in materials to keep it out of the public view.

I'm not familiar with the massive paintings in the Lincoln gallery, but there are a number of ways to get oversize works into an area. The most common is to bring the works in, in multiple pieces this is easy with digital prints and paintings as they can be delivered in rolls. One of the big questions when we are working on an estimate is about door sizes and elevator sizes, to make sure how big we can build pieces to bring in.
